questions.q: In the exercise's T-SQL query, what four Snowflake-relevant features appear?
options: TOP, string concatenation with +, a two-branch CASE, and a CTE wrapping ROW_NUMBER()
MERGE, stored procedures, transient tables, and Time Travel
Only window functions — nothing else differs from Snowflake
JOIN, WHERE, and GROUP BY, which all need to be rewritten
questions.explain: The exercise query was built specifically to touch TOP, string +, CASE, and a CTE-wrapped ROW_NUMBER() — the syntax points this chapter covered.

questions.q: How does TOP 100 in the original query get rewritten for Snowflake?
options: As LIMIT 100, moved to the end of the query after ORDER BY
As LIMIT 100 in the SELECT clause, in the same position as TOP
Snowflake has no way to limit rows, so it's simply removed
As TOP 100, unchanged, since Snowflake also supports TOP in that position
questions.explain: LIMIT is Snowflake's idiomatic row-limiting clause, placed at the end of the query after ORDER BY, unlike T-SQL's TOP in the SELECT clause.

questions.q: What replaces the CTE + ROW_NUMBER() + outer WHERE rn <= 3 pattern in the Snowflake rewrite?
options: QUALIFY rn <= 3, applied directly in the same query as the window function
A second CTE with an additional JOIN
MERGE INTO with a WHEN MATCHED clause
There is no way to replace this pattern in Snowflake
questions.explain: QUALIFY lets you filter on the ROW_NUMBER() result directly, eliminating the need for a wrapping CTE entirely.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should the JOIN, WHERE, and window function's PARTITION BY/ORDER BY clauses require when rewriting this query for Snowflake?
options: Zero changes — they are standard SQL that transfers directly between T-SQL and Snowflake
A complete rewrite using Snowflake-specific join syntax
Conversion to Snowflake Scripting stored procedure syntax
Removal, since Snowflake doesn't support multi-table joins
questions.explain: Only the syntax that actually differs (TOP, +, CASE, CTE+ROW_NUMBER) needs to change — joins, WHERE clauses, and window function syntax are identical in both dialects.

questions.q: What are the two recommended checks for verifying your own T-SQL-to-Snowflake rewrite?
options: Confirm both versions return the same row count, and confirm you changed only the syntax that actually differs
Run the query only in Snowflake and assume correctness if it doesn't error
Check that the query runs faster in Snowflake than in T-SQL
Confirm the column names were alphabetized
questions.explain: Matching row counts between both versions, plus a structural check that only the genuinely different syntax was touched, is the verification method this lesson recommends.
